q-113532.prompt: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
q-113532.solution:
First, let $u=@@D@@.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=@@A@@\,⟹\,\text{d}x=@@R@@\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot @@R@@\,\text{d}u \\  & =@@R@@\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+C & =@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =@@R@@(\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|@@D@@|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x=@@R@@\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|@@D@@|).
$$

q-72445.prompt: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
q-72445.solution:
First, let $u=@@D@@.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=@@A@@\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+C & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|-\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@D@@|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|@@D@@|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{@@D@@}\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|@@D@@|).
$$
